questions.question: How are label, name, value, and form submission connected in HTML?
questions.title: HTML form labels and submitted data
questions.direct_answer: A label gives a control an accessible name and connects through label[for] to the control's id. During submission, successful controls contribute name=value pairs: name is the request key and the current control value is its value. An id alone is not submitted, and disabled or unchecked checkbox controls are normally omitted.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner distinguishes DOM identity, accessible labelling, and submitted form data.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving an input only an id or placeholder and expecting it to be labelled and submitted.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain successful controls and the difference between disabled and readonly.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: label for must match the control id.
name becomes the submitted key; value becomes its submitted value.
A control without name is not included in form data.
Disabled controls and unchecked checkboxes are normally omitted.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A form control has two separate connections. Its label explains the control to people and assistive technology, while its name connects the control to submitted data. For an explicit label, the label's for value must exactly match the input's id.

The id identifies an element in the document; it is not the request key. When the form is submitted, each successful control contributes a name=value pair. An email input with name email and the value ana@example.com produces an email entry in FormData or the encoded request.

For example, clicking a correctly connected label focuses its text field and enlarges the clickable target of a checkbox. On submission, two radio buttons share one name so the selected value represents one field.

Controls without a name are not submitted. Disabled controls are omitted, and an unchecked checkbox normally contributes no pair at all. readonly is different: a read-only text control cannot be edited but can still be submitted.

The server must still validate every received value because the browser request can be changed outside the page. A placeholder is also not a replacement for a visible label; it disappears during typing and is not a dependable accessible name. A control may also be associated with a form elsewhere in the document through its form attribute. That changes which submission owns its data, but it does not change the separate jobs of label, id, name, and value.

sections.title: Identity, meaning, and transport
sections.content: id identifies a DOM element, label gives the control human meaning, name identifies the field in form data, and value is the current data. Keeping those jobs separate explains why a visually labelled input can still be absent from the submitted request.

sections.title: Only successful controls contribute data
sections.content: The submission algorithm builds entries from successful controls associated with the form. Control type and state matter: a checked checkbox contributes its value, the activated submit button can contribute its own name and value, and disabled controls are excluded. FormData is a useful way to inspect the exact entries without sending a network request.

sections.title: From visible field to request entry
sections.content:
label[for=email] -> input[id=email]  (accessible connection)
input[name=email] + current value    (data connection)
successful control -> FormData entry: email=ana@example.com

questions.question: How does built-in HTML form validation work?
questions.title: Built-in HTML constraint validation
questions.direct_answer: HTML constraint validation checks rules such as required, type, min, max, minlength, maxlength, and pattern on supported controls. An invalid form is blocked during normal submission and the browser exposes validity state and messages. Client validation improves feedback, but the server must repeat all security and business validation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands constraint validation as browser feedback rather than server-side security.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trusting a required or pattern attribute as protection against crafted requests.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect validity flags, accessible instructions, and repeated server validation.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Validation constraints come from control type and attributes.
Invalid controls can be styled with :invalid and inspected through validity.
checkValidity reports state; reportValidity also shows browser feedback.
Client-side validation never replaces server-side validation.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Built-in HTML validation uses constraints declared on form controls. required rejects an empty required value, type=email checks email syntax, min and max constrain numeric or date values, and pattern applies a regular expression to certain textual controls.

During a normal interactive submission, the browser checks candidate controls. If one is invalid, submission is blocked, the invalid event can fire, and the browser may focus the control and show a message. CSS pseudo-classes such as :valid and :invalid expose the state for styling.

JavaScript can read an input's validity object and validationMessage. checkValidity returns a boolean and fires invalid events; reportValidity also asks the browser to display its feedback. setCustomValidity adds a custom error, and passing an empty string clears it.

For example, an email field can be required and require a company domain with pattern. The label or nearby instructions should explain the rule before failure, and a custom message should identify what must change rather than saying only invalid input.

This is a usability layer, not a trust boundary. Attributes and JavaScript can be bypassed, requests can be sent directly, and some business rules need server data. The server repeats validation, returns field-specific errors, and must not rely on the browser for security. novalidate on the form or formnovalidate on a submitter can deliberately skip interactive browser validation. Those switches are useful for actions such as Save draft, but they never switch off the server's validation responsibility.

sections.title: Constraints produce a validity state
sections.content: Each candidate control has validity flags such as valueMissing, typeMismatch, patternMismatch, and rangeOverflow. The overall valid flag is true only when no constraint fails. Native submission uses that state automatically, while JavaScript can inspect it without rebuilding the rules.

sections.title: Native form-control semantics
sections.content: Native input types and attributes provide keyboard, mobile, and accessibility benefits beyond a regular expression. Custom validation should extend those semantics, not replace all controls with generic div elements. Keep error text associated with its field, preserve user-entered values, and move focus only when it improves recovery.

sections.title: Validation flow
sections.content:
Submit form
  -> browser evaluates eligible control constraints
  -> invalid? block submission + expose message/state
  -> valid? encode and send request
  -> server validates again in both cases

sections.title: Combine native rules with one clear custom message
sections.content:
```html

Use your @example.com address.

``` The browser checks presence, email syntax, and the declared pattern. The server must apply the same domain rule after submission.

questions.question: What is the difference between button, submit, and reset button types?
questions.title: HTML button types
questions.direct_answer: Inside a form, a button element without an explicit type behaves as type=submit. A submit button starts validation and form submission, type=button has no built-in form action and is used for scripted controls, and type=reset restores controls to their initial values. Explicit types prevent accidental submissions, and reset is rarely helpful in ordinary forms.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner knows the default type and the distinct native action of each button.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Leaving type off a secondary button and accidentally submitting the form.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention submitter name-value data and the requestSubmit versus submit distinction.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The default button type inside a form is submit.
type=submit validates and submits its associated form.
type=button performs no form action unless script adds one.
type=reset restores initial values and can erase work unexpectedly.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A button's type decides its default form behaviour. submit is the normal action button: it runs interactive constraint validation and, when valid, submits the associated form. A button element inside a form defaults to submit when type is omitted.

type=button has no built-in submission or reset behaviour. It is the right choice for a password-visibility toggle, an Add another field control, or another action handled by JavaScript.

type=reset restores form controls to the initial values defined when the page loaded or the form was reset. It does not mean clear every field, and it can erase a user's work with one accidental activation, so ordinary forms rarely need it.

For example, a Cancel button placed inside a form will unexpectedly submit unless it declares type=button. The Save control should declare type=submit so both actions remain obvious during maintenance.

A submit button can override form attributes such as action or method for that submission. The boundary is custom script: preventing a submit event changes the network action, but the button is still semantically a submit control and keyboard behaviour should remain intact.

sections.title: One element, three default actions
sections.content: submit hands control to the form submission algorithm, button waits for application logic, and reset restores initial control state. Declaring the type makes that contract visible and protects the form when a reusable button is moved inside it.

sections.title: The clicked submitter is part of the request
sections.content: The activated submit button can contribute its own name and value, allowing one form to distinguish Save draft from Publish. Scripted form.submit() and requestSubmit() differ: requestSubmit behaves like activating a submit button and performs validation, while form.submit() bypasses submit-event and interactive-validation steps.

sections.title: Default button behaviour
sections.content:
| type | Built-in action | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| submit | Validate and submit | Save, sign in, search |
| button | None | Scripted UI action |
| reset | Restore initial values | Rare specialised workflow |

sections.title: Prevent a secondary action from submitting
sections.content:
```html
<form>
  <label for="display-name">Display name</label>
  <input id="display-name" name="displayName" required>
  <button type="button" id="preview">Preview</button>
  <button type="submit">Save profile</button>
</form>
```
Preview has no implicit form action. Save remains the single control that starts validation and submission.

questions.question: When should an HTML form use GET instead of POST?
questions.title: Choosing GET or POST for HTML forms
questions.direct_answer: Use GET when submitting the form retrieves a representation without changing server state, such as search or filtering; the form data becomes part of the URL and can be bookmarked. Use POST when submission creates or changes state, sends a larger payload, or should not expose fields in the URL. HTTPS is still required because POST is not encryption.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner chooses an HTTP method from operation semantics.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming POST is secure by itself or using POST for every form.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain safe retrieval, bookmarkability, body encoding, and HTTPS as separate concerns.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: GET is appropriate for safe retrieval such as search and filters.
GET encodes form data in the URL query.
POST sends form data in the request body and is used for state changes.
Neither method makes data secret; HTTPS provides transport protection.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A GET form represents a safe retrieval. Its successful controls are encoded into the URL query, which makes the result linkable, bookmarkable, cache-friendly, and easy to reproduce. Search, filtering, and pagination are common examples.

A POST form sends its data in the request body and is normally used when the action creates or changes server state, such as creating an account, publishing a comment, or updating a profile. It also suits larger or structured submissions and file uploads with the correct encoding type.

For example, a product search with category and price filters should use GET so copying the result URL preserves those choices. A checkout confirmation should use POST because refreshing or repeating it can have an effect and the operation is not a safe retrieval.

POST does not hide data from the network and does not replace HTTPS. Request bodies can still appear in application logs or browser tooling, while GET fields can additionally appear in history, links, referrer data, and server logs.

The server owns method semantics and must protect state-changing requests against replay and cross-site request forgery where relevant. The form method is part of an HTTP contract, not simply a way to make the URL look cleaner.

sections.title: GET and POST form semantics
sections.content: The primary decision is whether repeating the request is intended only to retrieve information or may change state. URL visibility and payload shape matter, but they come after method semantics. A search should not become POST merely to avoid writing query parameters.

sections.title: Submission serializes successful controls
sections.content: Both methods begin with the same form data set. GET appends its encoded entries to the action URL. POST sends them in a request body using the chosen enctype, commonly application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data for files. The receiving endpoint must parse and validate the corresponding representation.

sections.title: GET and POST form behaviour
sections.content:
| Concern | GET | POST |
|---|---|---|
| Intended meaning | Safe retrieval | Processing or state change |
| Form data location | URL query | Request body |
| Bookmarkable result | Yes | Normally no |
| Needs HTTPS for privacy | Yes | Yes |

sections.title: Use the method that matches each operation
sections.content:
```html
<form action="/products" method="get">
  <label for="query">Search products</label>
  <input id="query" name="q">
  <button>Search</button>
</form>

<form action="/comments" method="post">
  <label for="comment">Comment</label>
  <textarea id="comment" name="comment" required></textarea>
  <button>Publish</button>
</form>
```
The search result can be shared through its query URL; publishing a comment is a state-changing POST operation.

questions.question: How do you build an accessible form with useful error messages?
questions.title: Accessible form labels and errors
questions.direct_answer: Give every control a persistent visible label, group related choices with fieldset and legend, place instructions before they are needed, and associate help or error text with the control using aria-describedby. Errors should identify the field and correction, remain visible, and never rely on color alone. Preserve entered values and validate again on the server.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can make labels, groups, instructions, and errors accessible in code.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using placeholders as labels or showing an unassociated red error message.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss recovery, preserved values, summaries, and restrained live announcements.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use a visible label correctly associated with every control.
Group radio buttons and checkboxes with fieldset and legend.
Associate instructions and errors with aria-describedby.
State what is wrong and how to correct it without color alone.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An accessible form begins with native controls and persistent visible labels. The label's for value matches the control id, which gives the field an accessible name and makes the label clickable. A placeholder may show an example but does not replace the label.

Related radio buttons or checkboxes belong in a fieldset with a legend that names the group. Required formats and constraints should be explained before input when possible, then connected to the control with aria-describedby.

When validation fails, the message identifies both the field and the repair. “Email must include @” is more useful than “Invalid value.” The message remains visible, is associated with the input, and is not communicated only through a red border.

For example, after a server rejects an account form, the page can show a summary linked to each invalid field and inline messages beside those fields. Existing values remain populated except sensitive fields, so the learner does not have to repeat valid work.

Focus management depends on the interaction. Moving focus to an error summary can help after a full submission, while live validation should not announce on every keystroke. Client-side feedback is only convenience; the server validates the same rules and returns errors in a form the page can associate correctly. I test the completed form with keyboard navigation and a screen reader, but I also read the submitted payload. Accessibility and data correctness meet at the same control associations.

sections.title: Name, describe, report, recover
sections.content: A usable form tells a person what each control is, what format is expected, what went wrong, and how to recover. Native HTML creates the strongest base because labels, groups, control states, and keyboard behaviour are already understood by browsers and assistive technology.

sections.title: Errors need a programmatic relationship
sections.content: Visual proximity helps sighted users, but aria-describedby lets a screen reader obtain the same help or error text while focused on the control. If the message element changes, aria-live may announce it, but repeated assertive announcements can become disruptive. An error summary is especially useful for long forms when its links move focus to the relevant controls.

sections.title: Accessible validation journey
sections.content:
Visible label + instructions
  -> user enters value with native control
  -> validation finds an issue
  -> inline message explains repair and is associated to field
  -> summary links to field when the form is long
  -> corrected value is validated by server

sections.title: Associate a clear error with its field
sections.content:
```html

Use the address where we can send the receipt.

Enter an email address containing @.

``` The label supplies the name; describedby connects both prior help and the current correction to the input.
